video.title: Hello, Python: print, text and numbers
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — the students’ computer studies teacher (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — the students’ maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Your phone can run real Python, the same language used by scientists, game makers and banks. Today you will write your first program. It will be one line long.
The instruction print shows something on the screen. Put text inside quotes and brackets, exactly like this. Press Run, and the computer does exactly what you wrote. That’s a program!
A program can have many lines. Python runs them one at a time, from the top down. Change the order of the lines, and the order on the screen changes too.
Python is also a calculator. Plus and minus are as you know them. A star means times, and a slash means divide. Two stars mean to the power of: two, star star, ten is one thousand and twenty-four.
Careful with quotes. With quotes, Python shows the text exactly as it is. Without quotes, it works the sum out. So the first line shows seven plus five, and the second shows twelve.
Quick check! The line is print, two plus three times four, with no quotes. What does it show?
Fourteen. Python follows the same order as maths: times and divide before plus and minus. If you want plus first, use brackets: two plus three, in brackets, times four is twenty.

With just print and maths, you can already do useful things. Work out how many minutes are in a school year. Print a poster for a school event. Check your maths homework. Find out how many seconds old you are.
Sometimes Python stops with a red error message. Don’t worry: everyone gets them. The last line says what’s wrong, and it tells you the line number. A missing quote or bracket is the most common.

scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: step through a program
scenes.narration: In the app, open Step through a program. Press Run and record, then Next, and watch Python run one line at a time. Then change the code to your own prints and sums, and run it again.
Your turn. What does print, with ten times two in quotes, show?

scenes.on_screen_text: print · top to bottom · quotes · times first
scenes.narration: Ten times two, just as written. Remember: print shows things on the screen. Python runs your lines from top to bottom. Text goes in quotes. And times comes before plus, unless you use brackets.
Try it yourself: work out how many hours you spend at school in a year, with one line of Python. Write your guess on paper first. Then run it, and see how close you were.

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — Python multiplies first, as in maths: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — times comes before plus, as in maths: 2 + 12 = 14.

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — in quotes it is text, so Python shows it exactly as written.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — quotes make it text, so nothing is worked out.
